phaseCues.intro: This is the briefing. You will meet the person on trial and learn the charge. Listen for what the prosecution must prove — you decide later if they proved it.
phaseCues.openings: Now you will hear openings. Each side tells its story of the case before any evidence is called. Notice what each side asks you to believe.
phaseCues.beats: Now the evidence. Witnesses and exhibits come one at a time. You do not decide yet — just listen carefully.
phaseCues.closings: Now the closings. Each side makes its final argument. After this, you retire with the jury to deliberate — you lock your own verdict only after that discussion.
phaseCues.verdict: If, after considering all the evidence, you are not sure the prosecution proved every element beyond reasonable doubt, your verdict must be Not Guilty.
phaseCues.juryroom: Welcome to the jury room. Under the fictional Aster Reach procedure used here, all 12 jurors first try to agree after three focused rounds. You may pause, reopen written notes, or raise a point. Then choose your own verdict. If the first ballot is not unanimous, the judge gives a neutral direction: keep considering each view without surrendering an honestly held one. Eleven matching votes can then return a verdict; undecided jurors remain undecided and may leave the jury hung.
phaseCues.reveal: This is the post-verdict review. Compare your reasoning with the authors’ reference verdict and the evidence they gave greatest weight. It is an editorial view, not a score.

speaker.direction: This is {name}, {role}. They will remind you of the legal rules that bind your decision.
speaker.exhibit: This is an exhibit, presented by {name}. Look at what it shows — and what it does not prove by itself.
speaker.cross: This is cross-examination of {name}. The other side will test their account. Listen for what holds up and what wobbles.
speaker.prosecution: This is {name}, {role}. Their job is to help prove the charge. Listen for the key facts they put forward.
speaker.defence: This is {name}, {role}. Their job is to raise doubt about the charge. Listen for the gaps they point out.
